result.markdown: --- title: "[maxcombo_test()]{.doc-object-name .doc-function .doc-label .doc-label-function}" body-classes: doc-api-page page-navigation: false html-table-processing: none --- ::: {.doc-subject} MaxCombo test: maximum of multiple weighted log-rank Z-statistics. ::: ::: {.doc-usage-source} Usage [Source](https://github.com/rich-iannone/greenwood/blob/feat-aft-residuals/greenwood/_tests.py#L552-L700){target="_blank" rel="noopener"} ::: ::: {.doc-signature .doc-Kind.FUNCTION} ```python maxcombo_test(surv, group, *, weights=None, strata=None) ``` ::: ::: {.doc-text} The MaxCombo test evaluates survival differences using several Fleming-Harrington weight functions simultaneously and takes the largest absolute Z-statistic as the test statistic. This makes it robust to unknown treatment-effect timing. When the effect is immediate, the standard log-rank (rho=0, gamma=0) dominates. When the effect is delayed, the late-emphasis weight (rho=0, gamma=1) dominates. The MaxCombo adapts automatically. **When to use**: When the proportional hazards assumption may not hold and you do not know in advance whether the treatment effect will be early, late, or sustained. This is common in immunotherapy and oncology trials where delayed effects are expected but not guaranteed. ::: ## Parameters {.doc-parameters} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [surv]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [Surv]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : A `Surv` response object (right-censored or counting-process). [group]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [Any]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : Group labels, one per observation. Must have exactly two unique levels. [weights]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [list[tuple[float, float]] | None]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [None]{.doc-parameter-default} : List of (rho, gamma) tuples defining the Fleming-Harrington weight functions. Defaults to the standard four-weight combo: `[(0, 0), (1, 0), (0, 1), (1, 1)]`, covering unweighted, early-emphasis, late-emphasis, and middle-emphasis tests. [strata]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [Any]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [None]{.doc-parameter-default} : Optional stratifying factor. When provided, each weighted test is stratified (computed within each stratum, then combined). ::: ## Returns {.doc-returns} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [MaxComboResult]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : A result object with attributes: - `statistic`: The maximum absolute Z-statistic across all weight functions. - `p_value`: P-value from the multivariate normal distribution. - `z_statistics`: Dictionary mapping each (rho, gamma) tuple to its Z-statistic. - `correlation`: Correlation matrix between the Z-statistics under H0. - `method`: Description of the test. ::: ## Details {.doc-details} The MaxCombo test is based on the joint distribution of the standardized weighted log-rank statistics under H0. Under the null hypothesis of equal survival, the Z-statistics are asymptotically multivariate normal with mean zero and a correlation matrix determined by the shared risk-set structure. The p-value is computed as $$ p = P\bigl(\max_j |Z_j| \ge T_{\mathrm{obs}}\bigr) = 1 - P\bigl(\text{all } |Z_j| < T_{\mathrm{obs}}\bigr), $$ where the probability is evaluated under the multivariate normal using Sobol quasi-Monte Carlo integration. ## References {.doc-references} Lee S.H. (2007). On the versatility of the combination of the weighted log-rank statistics. *Computational Statistics & Data Analysis*, 51(12), 6557-6564. ## Examples {.doc-examples} Test whether survival differs between the two sexes in the `lung` dataset using the default four-weight MaxCombo: ::: {#48baadf6 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.python .cell-code} import greenwood as gw lung = gw.load_dataset("lung", backend="polars") y = gw.Surv.right(lung["time"], event=(lung["status"] == 2)) result = gw.maxcombo_test(y, group=lung["sex"]) result ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` MaxComboResult(statistic=3.5657, p_value=0.0009956, weights=[(0, 0), (1, 0), (0, 1), (1, 1)]) ``` ::: ::: Examine which weight function produced the largest signal: ::: {#9fe2997c .cell execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code} result.z_statistics ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=2} ``` {(0, 0): 3.21352484896035, (1, 0): 3.565690872910549, (0, 1): 1.8601032675878904, (1, 1): 2.7685344459841996} ``` ::: ::: Use a custom weight set focusing on standard and delayed effects: ::: {#5aac0dd0 .cell execution_count=3} ``` {.python .cell-code} gw.maxcombo_test(y, group=lung["sex"], weights=[(0, 0), (0, 1)]) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=3} ``` MaxComboResult(statistic=3.2135, p_value=0.002224, weights=[(0, 0), (0, 1)]) ``` ::: :::
